newsitem.title: USA: U.S. plays down Bosnia differences with France.
newsitem.headline: U.S. plays down Bosnia differences with France.

text.p: U.S. officials said on Wednesday there have been disagreements with France over tactics for apprehending Bosnian war criminals but not over the "NATO consensus" on the need to bring suspects to justice.
"Have there been disagreements on tactics from time to time? Yes, there have," one U.S. official told Reuters, without going into detail.

But while Paris has changed its mind at different points during months of allied discussion on how best to arrest Bosnian war criminals, "I don't think the French have drawn any red lines" and talks continue, another official said.
The issue of France's willingness to go after the suspects was raised by a story in Wednesday's New York Times.
The newspaper said Paris declined to support NATO plans for a second raid to capture high-ranking Bosnian Serbs suspected of war crimes because the operation was too risky.
It quoted U.S. officials as saying NATO planned more raids to follow up last week's operation in Prijedor against two Serbs indicted for war crimes. One man was arrested and a second killed.

Citing U.S. and French officials, the paper said Paris was not opposed to the arrest of prominent Bosnian Serbs, who live and work in the Bosnian Serb stronghold of Pale but the French felt the plan under consideration was too risky.
Pale is headquarters of the Bosnian Serbs' wartime leader, Radovan Karadzic, and its former military chief, Ratko Mladic. Both were indicted by the war crimes tribunal at The Hague.
Pale is in the sector of Bosnia patrolled by French troops under the NATO-led peacekeeping force.
France denied the New York Times report, with Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt telling reporters: "This information has no basis."
In Washington, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns declined to label the story incorrect, although several officials said the matter was more complicated.

Burns insisted during repeated questioning at a news briefing that he was "not aware" that France had tried to block the NATO snatch operation against two indicted war criminals last week or any possible subsequent operation.
"I'm not aware the French have blocked any efforts since Prijedor. Not at all. No way," he said.
"I don't believe -- I'm not aware that the French were opposed to the Prijedor operation, no," he added.

He and other U.S. officials took pains to emphasise common goals and play down differences with Paris on the explosive and sensitive war criminals issue that Washington believes is crucial to peace in Bosnia.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, asked if war criminals could be brought to justice without France's active participation, ducked a straight answer.

"There is general agreement on the fact that war criminals need to be turned over to The Hague and there needs to be support for the war crimes tribunal," she told reporters at the start of talks with her Swedish counterpart.
This issue was discussed at the summit of the group of seven industrialised countries in Denver last month and again at the NATO summit in Madrid last week, she noted.
Albright also pointed to the French foreign ministry statement on Wednesday indicating support for "the concept" of turning war criminals over to The Hague.
"I think that it's very important to know there is NATO consensus on that," she said, calling it a "key part" of the 1995 Dayton peace accords that ended the Bosnian war.

The problem however is that the requirement that war criminals be sent to The Hague for trial is part of the Dayton accords and has been a NATO tenet since the Bosnian peace mission began. But until NATO took action at Prijedor -- when British troops moved to seize two men -- the alliance had not acted to take suspects into custody.

Rummelhardt said the main responsibility for seizing suspects lay with local authorities and French troops in the 31,000-strong NATO-led force "obey the rules of engagement set by NATO and follow the instructions of the force commander."
"We have always insisted on the need for suspects indicted by the war crimes tribunal to be arrested and transferred to this tribunal in The Hague," Rummelhardt said.
